name: Bluish Green
lede: Bluish Green is a pale, greyed green that earns its place from an 1821 naturalists' chart, where it was swatch number 51, matched to a thrush's egg.

sections.title: A naturalist's term
sections.body:
Bluish green is one of Werner's colors as Patrick Syme set them out for naturalists, number 51 in the greens [1]. Syme matched it to the egg of a thrush, to the underside of wild rose leaves and to beryl [1]. He took the term itself, with saffron yellow, lilac and blackish grey, from the English edition of Willdenow's botany textbook of 1805 [2].

Syme's chart, first published in 1814 and revised in 1821, was perhaps the only one English-speaking botanists used until 1886 [2]. The older Latin vocabulary had a word for the same zone: *glaucus*, which could mean grey-green, greenish or bluish green [3].

sections.title: Which swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here is the pale, greyed one: Werner's aged paper and the ISCC-NBS block 159, called pale green, which dates from 1955 [1]. It is mild, about 72 in lightness and only 11 in chroma [1]. Nearby names are [[celandine-green]], [[ash]] and [[cambridge-blue]] [1].

Other sources use the words for something far more vivid. The 2010 xkcd survey's bluish green is a saturated sea green, nothing like Syme's [1]. Treat the name as a direction, from [[green]] toward [[blue-green]], and not as one color.

sections.title: In the dictionary
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary reaches for the phrase constantly. A pale bluish green is aquamarine and a light one is spray, while colibri is a bluish-green also called humming-bird [4]. Tourmaline is a bluish green in his entry, and verde azzurro is a bluish-green pigment possibly made from malachite [4]. [[verdigris-green]] belongs here too, the film that forms on copper and bronze [4].

Ball gives the chemistry. Copper ions absorb in the red end of the spectrum, so copper salts look bluish-green, though how blue or how green depends on the neighbouring ions [5]. Green ultramarine, the intermediate stage of the artificial pigment, was described by Salter in 1869 as a bright bluish-green that dulls to greenish-blue on exposure [6]. Guignet's green, patented in 1859, is a bright bluish green too [4].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
Gage ties the hue to Gauguin, who came to prefer subtle close tones such as bluish-greens, purplish-reds and orange-yellows over Van Gogh's sharp contrasts [7]. [[painter:paul-gauguin|Gauguin]] does indeed lead our archive here, with [[painter:georges-seurat|Seurat]] and [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] [10].

Symbolism is thinner. In Mondrian's triptych *Evolution* of 1910 to 1911 the woman at left is bluish green, which a Theosophical chart reads as religious feeling tinged with fear [8]. That is one chart's code and not a general meaning. Birren claimed in 1950 that bluish greens are livable and flatter a complexion because they oppose it [9]. Birren's color opinions are contested, so take that as taste and not evidence.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Bluish Green appears in 421 of 23,781 paintings, 1.77 per cent, more common than 76 per cent of our named colors [10]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 1.8 per cent of 8,345 paintings, 1.5 times the museums' baseline [10]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 51 per cent of 283 paintings [10].

Seurat uses it in 5 of 41 works here, 4.0 times the baseline, and Gauguin and Monet follow [10]. The earliest match is from 1340, 481 years before the name was written down, which says only that the hue exists in old, aged paint [10]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.
